Softmax and gradient bandits

Instead of estimating values, an agent can keep a preference for each action and turn preferences into probabilities with the softmax function. Then it learns the preferences directly: push up the action just taken if the reward beat the average, push it down if not. This is the seed of every policy-gradient method in Lessons 70 onwards.

The maths

The softmax (Boltzmann) distribution turns preferences $H_t(a)$ into probabilities:

$$\pi_t(a) = \frac{e^{H_t(a)/\tau}}{\sum_{b} e^{H_t(b)/\tau}}$$

Every $\pi_t(a)$ is positive and they sum to 1. Adding a constant $c$ to every $H$ multiplies top and bottom by $e^{c/\tau}$, so only differences between preferences matter. As $\tau \to 0$ all the probability goes to the largest $H$; as $\tau \to \infty$ it spreads evenly. The gradient bandit uses $\tau = 1$.

After playing $A_t$ and receiving $R_t$, the gradient bandit algorithm (S&B §2.8) updates

$$\begin{aligned} H_{t+1}(A_t) &= H_t(A_t) + \alpha\,(R_t - \bar R_t)\,\big(1 - \pi_t(A_t)\big) \\ H_{t+1}(a) &= H_t(a) - \alpha\,(R_t - \bar R_t)\,\pi_t(a) \end{aligned}$$

The second line is for every action $a \ne A_t$.

$\bar R_t$ is the baseline: the average of the rewards before step $t$, with $\bar R_1 = R_1$ (S&B §2.8). A reward above it raises the chosen action's preference and lowers the rest. A reward below it does the opposite.

Why it works. The expected reward is $\mathbb{E}[R_t] = \sum_x \pi_t(x)\,q_*(x)$. The softmax derivative (with $\tau = 1$) is

$$\frac{\partial \pi_t(x)}{\partial H_t(a)} = \pi_t(x)\,\big(\mathbb{1}_{a = x} - \pi_t(a)\big)$$

where $\mathbb{1}_{a=x}$ is 1 if $a = x$ and 0 otherwise. These derivatives sum to 0 over $x$, so any baseline $B$ can be subtracted for free:

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial\, \mathbb{E}[R_t]}{\partial H_t(a)} &= \sum_x \big(q_*(x) - B\big)\,\pi_t(x)\,\big(\mathbb{1}_{a=x} - \pi_t(a)\big) \\ &= \mathbb{E}\Big[\big(q_*(A_t) - B\big)\big(\mathbb{1}_{a=A_t} - \pi_t(a)\big)\Big] \\ &= \mathbb{E}\Big[\big(R_t - \bar R_t\big)\big(\mathbb{1}_{a=A_t} - \pi_t(a)\big)\Big] \end{aligned}$$

The second line reads the sum as an average over $A_t \sim \pi_t$. The third uses $\mathbb{E}[R_t \mid A_t] = q_*(A_t)$ and takes $B = \bar R_t$. The update is one sample of this gradient times $\alpha$: stochastic gradient ascent on expected reward. The baseline does not change the expected update, but it shrinks its variance, which is why learning is so much faster with it.
